title: SAP Terminology and Structures for New Consultants

sections.title: Master Data vs Transaction Data
sections.text:
One of the most important distinctions in SAP is between master data and
transaction data. If learners understand this clearly early on, many later topics
become easier.
What is master data?
Master data is relatively stable, reference-type information that describes
business objects used repeatedly in processes. It does not represent a single
business event, but rather “who” or “what” the process is about.
Common examples:
Material master – describes a product or raw material (ID, description, base
unit of measure, valuation settings, etc.).
Customer master – describes a customer (name, address, payment terms,
sales area data).
Vendor/supplier master – describes a supplier (name, address, bank details,
payment terms).
G/L account master – defines an account in the chart of accounts (account
type, description, balance sheet or P&L classification).

Key characteristics of master data:
It is created and maintained but not “posted” like a transaction.
It is reused many times across documents and processes.
It affects how transactions behave (pricing, account determination, availability
checks, etc.).
Poor master data leads directly to process and reporting problems.
Think of master data as the “dictionary and structure” of your business in SAP.

sections.title: What is transaction data?
sections.text:
Transaction data records specific business events that happen at a point in time.
It is created as part of running the business: buying something, selling something,
moving stock, paying an invoice.
Examples:

A payment document clearing
open items.
A journal entry posting to G/L
accounts.
A vendor invoice or customer
invoice.
A goods movement (goods
receipt or goods issue).
A specific sales order for a
customer.
A specific purchase order
created on a given date for a
given vendor.
Master Data vs Transaction Data

sections.title: Characteristics of Transaction Data
sections.text:
Key characteristics of transaction data:
It is time-stamped and often linked to a period (posting date, document date).
It depends on master data (materials, customers, vendors, G/L accounts).
It forms the basis for operational tracking and financial reporting.
Once posted, it is typically not editable in a free-form way; corrections usually
require follow-up transactions.

sections.title: Why the Master Data vs Transaction Data Distinction Matters
sections.text:
Why this distinction matters
For consultants, the distinction matters because:
Many configuration and design decisions affect which data belongs in master
data vs what is captured in each transaction.
When troubleshooting, you must know whether an issue is due to wrong
master data (for example, wrong tax code on the customer master) or due to
incorrect transactional entry.

transaction migration.
A simple way to phrase it:
“Master data describes the entities involved; transaction data records what those
entities did.”

sections.title: Organizational Structure in SAP
sections.text:
SAP represents a company’s structure using various organizational units. These
are not just labels; they control how processes behave and how data is separated
and reported.
At bridge-module level, the goal is to understand the concept, not detailed
configuration.
Client
Highest-level environment in SAP.
Represents a complete business instance with its own master data and
configuration.
All other organizational units live inside a client.

Company code
Represents a legal entity for which a full set of financial statements (balance
sheet and P&L) can be produced.
Each company code has its own local currency, fiscal year variant, and
accounting-specific settings.
Many finance and controlling design decisions are made at company code
level.
In interviews, a common question is: “What is a company code?” A simple answer:
“A company code is the smallest organizational unit for which you can draw up
external financial statements in SAP.”

Plant

In trading, it might represent a distribution
center or main warehouse.
Materials are often planned and stocked at
plant level.
In manufacturing, it usually corresponds to a
factory.
Represents a location related to production,
procurement, or inventory.

Storage location
A more granular inventory location within a plant.
Used to organize materials physically and logically (for example, “Raw Material
Store,” “Finished Goods Warehouse”).

Sales organization (high-level view)
Represents a unit responsible for selling and distributing goods and services.
Used to structure sales reporting, pricing, and customer-facing activities.
Often combined with distribution channels and divisions in SD design (details
covered later in full training).

How organizational units connect
At a high level, you can imagine:
One client contains multiple company codes.
Each company code can have multiple plants.
Each plant can have multiple storage locations.
Each company code can be associated with one or more sales organizations
for SD processes.
The exact structure is tailored to each customer, but the principle is that SAP’s
organizational model must reflect the real-world structure of the enterprise so
that:
Processes can be executed correctly.
Data can be reported at the right levels (per company, plant, sales org, etc.).
Responsibility and control can be assigned clearly.

sections.title: Document Flow Thinking
sections.text:
SAP is a document-driven system. Each major step in a process usually creates a
document. Document flow is the way SAP links these documents into an
understandable chain that reflects the business story from start to finish.
Example: P2P document flow
A simple P2P flow might look like this:
1.Purchase Requisition (PR) – internal request to buy.
2.Purchase Order (PO) – formal commitment to the vendor.
3.Goods Receipt (GR) – confirmation that goods arrived.
4.Vendor Invoice – bill from the vendor.
5.Payment document – record of paying the vendor.

In SAP, you can often see the full chain from PR to payment. This allows users and
auditors to:

Verify that quantities and values are
consistent.
Confirm that approvals and controls
were respected.
Track why a purchase occurred.

Example: O2C document flow
A simple O2C flow might look like:
1.Sales Order (SO) – commitment to supply to a customer.
2.Delivery – logistics step for picking, packing, and shipping.
3.Goods Issue – removal of stock, recognizing that goods left the company.
4.Billing document / Invoice – bill sent to the customer.
5.Incoming payment document – receipt and clearance of customer payment.
Again, SAP can show the link from order to payment, helping users:
Answer customer queries (“Where is my order?”).
Check whether an order was billed and paid.
Analyze delivery and billing performance.

Why document flow matters for consultants
Thinking in document chains helps you:
Design end-to-end test cases instead of isolated steps.
Troubleshoot issues by walking the chain to see where something went
wrong.
Explain processes clearly to business users (“Your invoice did not appear
because the delivery was not posted.”).
Prepare compelling project stories in interviews (for example, explaining how
you tested P2P and O2C flows)

sections.title: Essential SAP Terms for beginners
sections.text:
This section summarizes key terminology every bridge-module learner should
know. These terms will appear repeatedly in configuration, testing, and project
discussions.
Transaction / transaction code (T-code)
A transaction in SAP is a function you execute (for example, posting an
invoice, creating a sales order).
A transaction code is a short identifier you can type into SAP GUI’s command
field to access that function (for example, FB60, ME21N, VA01).
In Fiori, many transactions are represented as apps instead of classic T-codes,
but the underlying business function is similar.

Posting
“Posting” means saving a document that creates entries in the database,
often with financial impact.
For example:
Posting a vendor invoice creates open items and accounting entries.
Posting a goods movement changes inventory and may affect value.
Once posted, documents are usually assigned unique numbers and may not
be freely editable; corrections require follow-up postings.

Clearing and open items
Open items are outstanding amounts that have not yet been cleared (for
example, unpaid vendor invoices or unpaid customer receivables).
Clearing is the process of matching and settling open items, such as:
Matching a vendor invoice with a payment.
Matching a customer invoice with an incoming payment.
Clearing marks items as settled and updates balances accordingly.

Configuration vs customization
Configuration
Adjusting standard SAP settings to fit a business (for example, defining
document types, number ranges, account determination).
Usually done via SPRO or similar customizing tools, without changing
underlying code.
Customization / development
Writing new code, user exits, enhancements, or interfaces when standard
behavior is not enough.
Usually done by technical consultants (ABAP, integration, etc.).
Functional consultants are primarily responsible for configuration and for
specifying what kind of customization is needed, if any.

Posting period and fiscal year
Posting period – a defined time interval (e.g., month) during which financial
documents can be posted.
Fiscal year – the 12-month cycle used for financial reporting; it can align with
the calendar year or differ (such as April–March).
Posting periods are tightly controlled to ensure that financial statements are
complete and stable for closed periods.

Posting period Fiscak year

Chart of accounts (high-level)
The chart of accounts is the structured list of all G/L accounts used by a
company or group.
It defines how transactions are categorized for reporting (assets, liabilities,
income, expenses).
In SAP, G/L account master data refers to entries in the chart of accounts.

sections.title: How this chapter supports your implementation
sections.text:
This terminology and structural understanding is not just for passing a quiz. It
directly influences how you think and speak as a consultant:
When a business user describes a problem, you can recognize whether it
relates to master data, transaction data, organizational structure, or
document flow.
When you design or test a process, you know which organizational levels
(company code, plant, storage location, sales org) must be considered.
When you describe your work in interviews, you can use accurate SAP
terminology, which signals credibility and readiness.
